extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in academic publishing, science/humanities debates, and scholarly ethics
extracted.subtask_description: A encyclopedic case study of the 1996 Sokal affair describing the hoax, publication process, reactions, and its implications for evaluating scholarship, editorial practice, and academic ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a journal exercises sufficient intellectual rigor in evaluating submissions (Sokal's experiment was to test the journal's intellectual rigor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that what should matter is analysis of evidence and arguments, not only the article's sounding 'good' or flattering editors' preconceptions. Sokal claimed editors 'felt no need to analyze the quality of the evidence, the cogency of the arguments, or even the relevance of the arguments to the purported conclusion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of peer review / external expert review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether submissions are subjected to academic peer review or outside expert review by knowledgeable specialists in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social Text did not practice academic peer review at the time and did not submit Sokal's article for outside expert review by a physicist; the absence of peer review is presented as a factor in the hoax succeeding and as a standard editors might use to judge technical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the adequacy and reliability of the evidence provided to support claims in a scholarly article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sokal criticized the editors for not analyzing 'the quality of the evidence' supporting the article's claims; editorial evaluation should include scrutiny of evidence rather than only stylistic or ideological fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cogency of arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the arguments in a submission are logically coherent, well-supported, and persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sokal highlighted that editors apparently did not assess the 'cogency of the arguments'; cogent reasoning is a criterion distinguishing serious scholarship from nonsense or parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of arguments to claimed conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the presented arguments actually bear on and support the conclusions the author claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes editors 'felt no need to analyze ... the relevance of the arguments to the purported conclusion,' implying relevance is a necessary evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial bias / ideological obsequiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether editorial decisions are influenced by ideological alignment or flattering the editors' preconceptions rather than merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sokal's hypothesis was that the article would be published if it 'sounded good' and 'flattered the editors' ideological preconceptions.' The affair is used to question acceptance driven by ideological fit rather than substantive merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing quality and editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The readability, style, and compositional quality of an article and whether editors enforce standards (e.g., excising excessive speculation or footnotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social Text's editors later said they had requested changes to 'excise a good deal of the philosophical speculation' and 'excise most of his footnotes,' indicating writing quality and appropriate editorial revision are part of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical behavior in submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether deceptive practices by authors (e.g., deliberate hoaxes) violate ethical norms of scholarly conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors accused Sokal of behaving unethically in deceiving them. The article raises the question of whether Sokal was wrong to deceive editors or readers as part of his experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority/credential-based acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to publish work because of the author's academic credentials or perceived authority rather than solely on content quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social Text published the piece partly 'because of Sokal's credentials' and because he was an academic seeking affirmation, illustrating a criterion where perceived author prestige can override critical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing parody/satire from earnest scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of editors and reviewers to detect whether a piece is sincere scholarship or deliberately absurd/parodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors later said they did not suspect the piece was a parody; Sokal argued their failure to detect parody evidenced lack of critical examination. Detecting genre (parody vs. scholarship) is therefore an evaluative concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct and careful use of scientific terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding misuse or gratuitous borrowing of scientific terms and ensuring technical terms are used appropriately and accurately in non-scientific disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sokal and Bricmont's follow-up work criticized intellectuals for misusing scientific terminology; the affair highlights the criterion that interdisciplinary claims should use science terms properly or consult experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to confirmatory/selection bias in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of and protection against audiences or editors applying less stringent standards when critiquing targets they already view unfavorably (confirmatory bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites scholarship (Hilgartner) arguing that audiences may apply less stringent standards of evidence and ethics to attacks on targets they regard unfavorably, meaning evaluators should guard against such asymmetric standards.
